paper.abstract_en: Quantum gas microscopy provides single-shot access to many-body configurations, yet has so far relied on pinning atoms to a discrete lattice during fluorescence readout. Here, we realize ultrafast atom-resolved fluorescence microscopy of an ultracold $^{162}$Dy gas directly in free space, with all external confinement removed during imaging. Exploiting the large mass and broad optical transition of dysprosium together with a high numerical aperture in-vacuum objective, we detect single atoms within $4\,μ\mathrm{s}$ while maintaining an effective point-spread function with a full width at half maximum of $254.8(3)\,\mathrm{nm}$. We achieve a single-atom conditional classification fidelity of $99.72(3)\%$ for identified fluorescence candidates. We use the measured single-atom response to construct a statistical configuration-inference model that recovers atomic positions and multiplicities, coming from overlapping atoms, directly from single fluorescence snapshots. We further benchmark our reconstruction algorithm through end-to-end Monte Carlo simulations with known ground-truth atomic configurations, obtaining a reconstruction fidelity of $98.7\%$. Our approach, applicable to a wide variety of atomic species, extends quantum gas microscopy beyond predefined detection lattices, enabling atom-resolved measurements of counting statistics and higher-order spatial correlations directly on the intrinsic length scales of continuum many-body systems.
